description_full: First Horizon Corporation operates as the bank holding company for First Horizon Bank that provides various financial services. It operates through Regional Banking, Specialty Banking, and Corporate segments. The company offers commercial banking, business banking, consumer banking, private client investment, wealth management, financial planning, trust and asset management services, asset-based lending, commercial real estate, equipment finance/leasing, energy finance, international banking, healthcare finance, transportation and logistics finance, treasury management solutions, and loan syndications services. It also provides fixed income securities sales, trading, underwriting, and strategies for institutional clients; loan sales; portfolio advisory services; derivative sales; mortgage warehouse lending; franchise finance; corporate and correspondent banking; and mortgage origination services. Further, it provides transaction processing services, credit card products, and sale of mutual funds. First Horizon Corporation was formerly known as First Horizon National Corporation and changed its name to First Horizon Corporation in April 2004. The company was founded in 1864 and is headquartered in Memphis, Tennessee.

financial_summary: First Horizon Corporation is a large-cap financial services business with a $10.9B market cap on $3.4B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +11% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory. Operating margins are expanding by +2.3pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 11% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $595M in free cash flow — roughly 17 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.64×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.0× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 0.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 11.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 37% operating margin runs 8pp above the Financial Services median (29%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.44x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-4.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.02 across 512 companies in the universe; the top four hold 20% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 12% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 9% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 13% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 22% and a beta of 0.84, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.49 vs 5y 0.76), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $119.7M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 60% in the 2020 crash, 12% in the 2022 bear market and 76% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $13.06 (margin of safety -76%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 24%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $10.22 to $16.97 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Financial Services peers: P/E 16.7 vs 12.2 and P/FCF 18.3 vs 12.9 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-2%).
The 21 covering analysts target $27.13 on average, 18% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 4.6% annual cash-flow growth, 8pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 11% earns above the cost of capital of 8.9%, but the 2pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.64).
It converts 17% of revenue into free cash flow.
As a lender it runs a net interest margin of 3.55% and an efficiency ratio of 55%.
It earns a 11% return on equity.
hlth: CET1 capital of 11.2% sits comfortably above the ~7% regulatory minimum with buffer.
Non-performing loans are 0.83% of the book, a clean credit profile.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 2.2% over 3 years, 1.6% over 5 years and 11.3% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 21%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 5.9% on average.
Analysts expect 8.5% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (1.0%), and institutions hold 90%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (5 sales, net $455K sold).
It returns 11.3% a year to shareholders (8.4% in buybacks and 3.0% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 15 consecutive years, raising it 7.2% a year over the last five.
people: With about 7,375 employees, each generates about $464K of revenue, in line with the Financial Services median, and productivity has risen 4.8% a year.
That works out to $81K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.5M (8x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
